concept.name: Pearson correlation
concept.definition: The standardized measure of linear association between two variables, equal to their covariance divided by the product of their standard deviations, ranging from -1 (perfect negative linear) to +1 (perfect positive linear). Developed by Karl Pearson around the early 1900s.
concept.intuition: It measures how well a straight line describes the relationship: +1 or -1 means all points lie exactly on a line, 0 means no linear pattern at all.
concept.mechanics: Standardize each variable (subtract its mean, divide by its standard deviation), multiply the paired standardized values, and average. The sign matches the slope of the least-squares regression line, and r^2 is the share of variance in y explained linearly by x.
concept.formula: r = [n*SUM(xy) - (SUM x)(SUM y)] / sqrt( [n*SUM x^2 - (SUM x)^2] * [n*SUM y^2 - (SUM y)^2] ), where n is the number of paired observations.
concept.failure_modes: It detects only linear structure: U-shaped, cyclical, or threshold relationships can yield r near 0 despite perfect dependence. It is also non-robust - one outlier can inflate or destroy r - and it presumes the relationship is stable over the sample.
concept.misconceptions: r = 0 does not mean 'no relationship', only no linear one. Squaring r gives variance explained, so r = 0.5 means only 25% shared variance, not '50% association'; and strong correlation still does not imply causation.
concept.example: For 11 students' third-exam and final-exam scores, OpenStax computes r = 0.6631, so r^2 = 0.44: about 44% of the variation in final scores is linearly explained by third-exam scores.
